articles.title: Best Badminton Rackets for Beginners (2026) - What to Buy First
articles.headline: Best Badminton Rackets for Beginners (2026)
articles.metaDescription: The best beginner badminton rackets in 2026. What balance point, shaft flex and 4U actually mean, why a stiff racket makes you worse, and which rackets are worth buying first.

body.text: Badminton rackets are described in a private language — 4U, head-heavy, medium flex, isometric — and none of it is explained on the box. The result is that most people buy their first proper racket on price and brand, discover it feels worse than the aluminium one they borrowed, and quietly conclude they are the problem.

They usually are not. The most common beginner mistake is buying a racket that is too stiff, and a stiff racket genuinely does make a developing player worse. Here is what the terms mean, and what to buy.
The Three Things That Actually Matter

A badminton racket is defined by balance, flex and weight. Balance is where the mass sits — head-heavy hits harder and swings slower, head-light swings faster and hits softer. Flex is how much the shaft bends under load. Weight is written backwards, as a U number, where bigger means lighter.

Everything else on the listing — frame technology names, string tension claims, colour schemes — is either marketing or something you can change later. If you match those three properties to how you play, a $35 racket beats a $200 one in the wrong hands.
Why a Stiff Shaft Makes a Beginner Worse

This is the part worth understanding properly, because it is counter-intuitive. A racket shaft works like a spring: your arm accelerates the handle, the shaft bends backwards, and then it snaps forward and whips the head through the shuttle. That whip is a real, measurable part of where power comes from.

A stiff shaft only bends if you swing fast enough to bend it. Swing at ordinary club speed with a stiff racket and it simply never loads — you get no whip, the shuttle leaves slowly, and the racket feels dead in your hand. Meanwhile a flexible shaft loads at that same speed and gives the energy back.

So the expensive stiff racket that a professional uses to generate 200mph smashes will, held by someone still learning to clear, produce shots that land mid-court. Buy flexible or medium flex until your clears reach the back line reliably.
Head-Heavy or Head-Light: Pick by How You Play

Head-heavy rackets put mass out at the end of the lever, which is why they smash harder — but the same mass makes them slower to bring round for the next shot. Head-light rackets reverse both. This is not a quality difference; both exist at every price.

If you play singles, or you are the person at the back of a doubles court hitting down, head-heavy suits you. If you play doubles at the net where rallies are fast and flat, head-light suits you. If you genuinely do not know yet — and most beginners do not — buy even balance and find out.
4U Is the Answer to the Weight Question

Badminton weight classes run in reverse: 3U is roughly 85-89g, 4U is 80-84g, and 5U is 75-79g. 4U has become the default and it deserves to be. It is light enough to swing repeatedly through a long rally without your forearm giving up, and heavy enough that the shuttle notices.

Go 3U only if you specifically want more mass behind a smash and have the arm to move it. Go 5U if your wrist tires quickly or you play at the net in mixed doubles. Otherwise 4U, and stop thinking about it.
The Rackets Worth Buying

The sensible floor of the market and the right amount to risk on a sport you are still trying. It is aluminium rather than graphite so it will never feel crisp, but the head is isometric and the shaft genuinely flexes — the two things that the rackets bundled with garden net sets get wrong. That is enough racket to learn a clear, a drop and a serve on properly. Treat it as a twelve-month racket, not a keeper.

If you want one recommendation and no further discussion, this is it. The Hi-Flex shaft loads at an ordinary club swing speed rather than a professional one, which is exactly the point made above — it gives energy back to a normal arm instead of demanding a faster one. Head-light balance means the racket arrives early, which is the difference between blocking a smash and watching it go past. Twenty thousand-odd buyers have reached the same conclusion.

Full graphite, one-piece, 76 grams, at a price where most rackets are still aluminium hybrids. The one-piece T-joint matters more than the spec sheet suggests: on a glued-joint racket the head twists independently of the shaft when you hit off-centre, and on this one it does not. The finish tells you it is not a Yonex. The part you hit shuttles with is right.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Buy the Yonex GR 303i if you are still finding out whether you like badminton. Buy the Nanoray 10F if you already know you will keep playing — it is the racket that ends most people's search. Buy the Senston N80 if you want full carbon and would rather spend the difference on shuttles. Do not buy a stiff, head-heavy racket as your first proper one, however good the reviews are.
What to Spend the Rest of Your Money On

Once you have a racket, the next two purchases both cost under fifteen dollars and change more than a racket upgrade would. The first is a tube of decent nylon shuttles, because the shuttles bundled with sets fly badly enough to teach you wrong habits. The second is an overgrip, because every racket under $50 ships with a moulded handle that goes slippery the moment your hands warm up.

After that, court shoes — badminton is played on a wooden floor with constant lateral push-off, and running shoes have neither the grip pattern nor the lateral support for it. That is a genuine injury point rather than a performance one.

faq.q: How much should a beginner spend on a badminton racket?
faq.a: Between $25 and $40. Below about $20 you are buying an aluminium frame on a steel shaft that flexes in the wrong place, and shots feel mushy no matter what you do. Above about $60 you are paying for a stiffer shaft that a developing swing cannot load, which makes the racket feel worse rather than better. The $25 to $40 band buys an isometric head and a flexible shaft, which is everything a beginner needs.

faq.q: Is a head-heavy or head-light racket better for a beginner?
faq.a: Even balance, unless you already know how you like to play. Head-heavy rewards people who attack from the back court and punishes slow hands at the net; head-light does the reverse. A beginner has not yet found out which they are, and an even-balance racket does neither thing badly. You can buy the specialised one as your second racket, once the answer is obvious.

faq.q: What does 4U mean on a badminton racket?
faq.a: It is the unstrung weight class, numbered in reverse: 3U is about 85 to 89 grams, 4U is 80 to 84 grams, and 5U is 75 to 79 grams. 4U is the modern default because it balances swing speed against the mass you need to actually move the shuttle. Unless you have a specific reason to want a heavier or lighter frame, 4U is correct.

faq.q: Should a beginner buy a pre-strung racket?
faq.a: Yes. Factory stringing sits around 20 lbs, which is a sensible middle tension, and it saves $20 to $25 on top of the racket price. Buying an unstrung frame only makes sense once you know what tension you want — and you cannot know that until you have played enough to notice the difference between power and control.

faq.q: Are cheap badminton rackets from a set any good?
faq.a: For social garden play, they are fine. For learning the sport, they are actively unhelpful: the aluminium-head-on-steel-shaft construction bends in the middle rather than whipping through, so the shuttle has already left before the frame has finished flexing. Players who learn on them develop an arm-heavy swing to compensate and then have to unlearn it.

articles.title: Badminton Gear: The Complete Beginner Guide (2026)
articles.headline: Badminton Gear: The Complete Beginner Guide
articles.metaDescription: Everything a new badminton player needs and nothing they do not. What to buy first, what to skip, realistic budgets from $60 to $250, and the order to buy things in.

body.text: Badminton is one of the cheapest sports in the world to start and one of the easiest to overspend on, because the equipment list looks short and every item has a $200 version. This guide covers what you actually need, in the order you actually need it.
The short version: a racket, shuttles and court shoes will get you playing properly for about $80. Everything else on this page is an upgrade, not a requirement.
What You Need on Day One

items: A racket — $25 to $40 buys a genuinely playable one
Non-marking indoor shoes — most halls require them, and it is a real injury issue
An overgrip — two dollars, and it fixes the slippery handle every cheap racket has

body.text: That is the whole list. Nets are provided at any club or leisure centre, and if you are playing in a garden the net comes with the garden set. Clothing is whatever you already own that you can sweat in.
The Racket: Flexible Beats Expensive

The single most useful thing to know about a beginner racket is that shaft flex matters more than price. A flexible shaft bends under an ordinary swing and snaps forward, doing part of the work for you. A stiff shaft only does that if you swing hard enough to bend it, which most new players cannot — so the expensive racket produces slower shots than the cheap one.
Buy flexible or medium flex, even balance, 4U weight class. Our beginner racket guide goes through the terminology in detail.

The Hi-Flex shaft is the whole point: it loads at a normal club swing speed instead of demanding a professional one, so you get the whip that generates power rather than fighting a stiff frame. Head-light balance means it arrives early enough to block a smash. It is the racket that most often ends the search for people who keep asking what to buy first.
Shuttles: Buy Nylon, Try Feather Once

This is where new players waste money in both directions. Some buy the cheapest nylon shuttles going, which fly flat and hard and teach nothing. Others buy feather because it is what the professionals use, then destroy a $25 tube in one session of mis-hits.

The right pattern is to train on good nylon — the Yonex Mavis range is the reference — and buy one tube of feather so you know what real badminton flight feels like. Once you have seen a feather drop shot brake over the net, you will understand what the sport is built around. Then go back to nylon for practice.

The default training shuttle in club halls worldwide, and the one you will be handed if you turn up somewhere new. The skirt is softer than budget nylon, so it deforms and brakes slightly on impact rather than sailing — noticeably closer to feather behaviour at a fraction of the running cost. Consistency tube to tube matters more than it sounds: practising drops against shuttles that all brake differently teaches you nothing.
Shoes Are Not Optional, and Running Shoes Are Not Shoes

Badminton is a lateral sport played on a sprung wooden floor. Almost every movement is a push off the side of the foot, followed by a stop. Running shoes are built to roll forward and have soft, tall midsoles that let the ankle tip over sideways — which is precisely the injury badminton produces.

Court shoes have a flat, gum-rubber sole for grip on wood, a low profile so the ankle stays over the foot, and lateral reinforcement in the upper. Most sports halls also require non-marking soles as a condition of entry. This is the one item on the list where buying the wrong thing has a physical cost, and it is worth $50 to $70.
The Two-Dollar Upgrade Everyone Skips

Every racket under about $50 comes with a moulded synthetic base grip that becomes slippery the moment your hands warm up. An overgrip — a thin tape you wrap over the top — fixes it completely, costs a dollar or two, and lasts a few weeks.

There are two families. Tacky grips stick to your hand and suit dry hands and cool halls. Perforated or dry grips absorb sweat and suit hot halls and people whose hands sweat. Buy a multi-pack of either; buying them one at a time is how people end up playing on a worn grip for a year.

Super GRAP is the reference point every other overgrip is measured against — tacky without being sticky, thin enough not to bulk out the handle, and consistent from roll to roll. Bought in a 30-pack it costs about the same per grip as the cheapest generics, which removes the only reason not to use it. Thirty is two or three years for one player.
Realistic Budgets
$60-$80 — Getting Started

A $27 aluminium racket, a $10 tube of nylon shuttles, a $2 overgrip and whatever trainers you own that are non-marking. This is enough to play at a club for a few months and find out whether you want to continue. Do not skip the overgrip.
$150-$180 — Playing Properly

A $40 graphite racket with a flexible shaft, $60 court shoes, a $16 tube of Mavis shuttles, a multi-pack of overgrips and a $30 sling bag. This covers everything and nothing here will need replacing for a couple of years except the consumables.
$250+ — Committed

Add a second racket so a broken string does not end your evening, a proper kit-bag with a shoe compartment, a tube of feather shuttles for matches, and a restring at your preferred tension. At this point the equipment stops being the limiting factor.
What to Skip

items: A $150+ racket as your first — stiff shafts need a swing speed you do not have yet
Feather shuttles for practice — you will destroy them and learn nothing extra
Anti-vibration gadgets — badminton frames barely vibrate; this is a tennis product
Wrist weights and 'power trainers' — badminton power comes from technique and rotation, not from strengthening the swing you already have wrong
A four-racket garden set, if only one person plays — the money goes into three frames nobody uses

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Spend $40 on a flexible-shaft racket, $16 on decent nylon shuttles, $60 on proper court shoes and $2 on an overgrip. That is a complete, genuinely good badminton setup for under $120, and the only thing on it you will replace this year is the shuttles. Buy the expensive racket after you know whether you attack from the back or defend at the net.

faq.q: How much does it cost to start playing badminton?
faq.a: About $60 to $80 for a workable setup — a $27 racket, $10 of nylon shuttles, a $2 overgrip and non-marking shoes you may already own. Around $150 buys a setup that will not need upgrading: a graphite racket, proper court shoes and better shuttles. Court hire at a leisure centre is usually the larger ongoing cost, not the equipment.

faq.q: Do I need special shoes for badminton?
faq.a: Yes, and this is the one item worth insisting on. Badminton is played with constant sideways push-off on a wooden floor, and running shoes have tall soft midsoles that let the ankle roll over. Court shoes are flat, grippy on wood and reinforced laterally. Most sports halls also require non-marking soles to use their floor at all.

faq.q: What should I buy first for badminton?
faq.a: A racket and a tube of nylon shuttles, then court shoes, then an overgrip. In practice most people get the first two immediately and put off shoes, which is the wrong order if you are playing on a wooden floor more than occasionally — the shoes are the injury item.

faq.q: Do I need to buy a badminton net?
faq.a: Only if you are playing at home. Every club, leisure centre and school hall provides nets and marked courts. A portable net is a garden purchase, and if that is what you want, our nets and posts page covers what makes one stay upright.

faq.q: How long does badminton equipment last?
faq.a: A graphite racket lasts years unless you clash it with a partner's. Strings go dead in months regardless of whether they break. Nylon shuttles last weeks; feather shuttles last a game or two. Court shoes lose their grip pattern after about a year of regular play, which is the point at which they stop being court shoes.

articles.title: Feather vs Nylon Shuttlecocks: Which Should You Buy? (2026)
articles.headline: Feather vs Nylon Shuttlecocks: Which Should You Buy?
articles.metaDescription: Feather and nylon badminton shuttlecocks compared. How the flight differs, what each actually costs per hour, speed ratings explained, and which one is right for where you play.

body.text: This is the only genuine fork in badminton equipment, and it is not a quality question. Feather shuttles are not the good ones and nylon the cheap ones — they fly differently, cost differently, and are correct in different places.
The short answer: nylon for practice and anywhere outdoors, feather for indoor matches. Here is why, and what it actually costs.
The Flight Is Genuinely Different

A feather shuttle is sixteen goose or duck feathers glued into a cork base. The skirt is porous and slightly irregular, which creates enormous drag the moment the shuttle slows down. So a feather shuttle leaves the racket fast and then brakes hard — that steep, almost vertical drop at the end of its flight is what makes badminton's drop shots and net play work as a game.

A nylon shuttle has a moulded one-piece skirt. It is smoother, more rigid, and produces less drag at low speed, so it carries further and flattens out instead of dropping. The practical effect is that shots which should die over the net instead land at the service line, and clears that should sit down instead sail long.
None of this makes nylon bad. It makes it a different flight model, and one that happens to be much better suited to wind, concrete and beginners.
Durability Is the Real Trade

A feather shuttle can be finished in a single rally. Feathers split when they are hit by a frame rather than strings, and a split feather changes the flight immediately even though the shuttle looks intact. Club players at a decent standard typically budget roughly one shuttle per game.

A nylon shuttle survives being mis-hit, trodden on, played on grass and left in a bag for six months. Recreational players get weeks or months out of one, and it usually dies from a cracked skirt or a squashed cork rather than from wear.

Put those together and the cost per hour is not close. A $23 tube of twelve feather shuttles might cover two or three club evenings. A $16 tube of six Mavis nylon shuttles covers a season of the same play.
Speed Ratings Are About the Room, Not About You
Both types are sold as slow, medium or fast, and this confuses nearly everyone the first time. It is not a difficulty setting and it is not about how hard you hit. It is a correction for air density.

Cold, thin, high-altitude air produces less drag, so a shuttle carries further and you need a slower one. Hot, humid, sea-level air produces more drag, so you need a faster one. The standard test is a full-power underarm clear from the back tramline: the shuttle should land between the back doubles service line and the baseline.
For a heated indoor hall at ordinary altitude, medium or slow is right. If you are guessing, buy medium.
What to Buy for Where You Play
Garden, driveway or park

Nylon, and the heavier outdoor variety if there is any breeze at all. Feather shuttles in wind are simply unplayable — they weigh under 5 grams and a light gust moves them a metre. This is not a compromise; it is the only workable option.

A heavier base than the cheapest nylon shuttles, which does two useful things outside: it fights a light breeze instead of stalling, and it keeps flying when a beginner hits it softly. Nowhere near feather flight, and it does not need to be — for a driveway or a park these will outlast a whole summer of casual games without anyone caring where they land.
Club training and practice

Good nylon. The gap between cheap hard nylon and a proper Mavis-grade skirt is larger than the gap between good nylon and feather for training purposes, because what you need from a practice shuttle is consistency — every shuttle in the tube braking at the same point.

The cheapest Yonex shuttle worth owning, and the point where nylon stops being a compromise and starts being a choice. The skirt is softer than budget nylon, so it deforms on impact and recovers — which produces a small but real braking effect that budget shuttles do not have. If you train twice a week, this is the shuttle to train on.
Indoor matches

Feather, if you can afford the running cost. There is no substitute for the way a feather shuttle brakes, and tactics built on nylon flight do not transfer cleanly. If your club plays matches on feather, practise on feather occasionally so the timing is not a surprise.

Feather flight without the tournament-brand price, which for most club players is the correct trade. The braking curve is the real thing — drops die over the tape instead of drifting to the service line — and the cork base gives the crisp report off the strings that nylon never manages. Expect to use them up. That is what feather is.
Storing Feather Shuttles

Feathers are organic and they dry out. A tube left in a hot car or a dry heated room for a month produces shuttles that shatter on the first clean smash, and people almost always blame the manufacturer for this.

The standard fix is humidity: keep the tube sealed, store it somewhere cool, and before a session put a slightly damp cloth or sponge in the tube for a few hours. Rehydrated feathers are flexible again and survive normally. Nylon needs none of this, which is another quiet argument for training on it.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: If you play outdoors or you are still learning, buy nylon and buy the good nylon rather than the cheapest — the flight consistency is what you are paying for. If you play indoor club matches, buy feather and accept it as a running cost of roughly one shuttle per game. Buy one tube of feather regardless, just so you know what the sport is supposed to feel like.

faq.q: Are feather shuttlecocks better than nylon?
faq.a: They fly the way the sport was designed around — braking hard at the end of the flight, which is what makes drop shots and net play work. But they are destroyed quickly, cost far more per hour, and are unusable outdoors or in any wind. Better is the wrong frame: feather is correct for indoor matches, nylon is correct for practice and outdoors.

faq.q: How long does a feather shuttlecock last?
faq.a: Anywhere from a single rally to a couple of games. Feathers split when hit by the frame rather than the strings, and a split feather changes the flight immediately even if the shuttle looks fine. Club players at a decent standard typically budget about one shuttle per game, which is why clubs pool the cost rather than individuals buying them.

faq.q: Why do my feather shuttlecocks break so quickly?
faq.a: Usually because they are too dry rather than defective. Feathers are organic and lose flexibility in dry heated air, then shatter on the first solid hit. Store tubes sealed and cool, and put a damp sponge or cloth in the tube for a few hours before a session. Mis-hits off the frame are the other cause, and that one only technique fixes.

faq.q: What speed shuttlecock should I buy?
faq.a: Medium, unless you know your hall is unusually hot or cold. Speed corrects for air density, not skill — cold thin air needs a faster shuttle, hot humid air needs a slower one. Test with a full underarm clear from the back tramline: it should land between the back doubles service line and the baseline.

faq.q: Can I use nylon shuttlecocks for competitive badminton?
faq.a: For club and league play, often yes — many leagues specify nylon precisely to control costs, and Yonex Mavis shuttles are the usual standard. Sanctioned tournament badminton is played on feather. If you are training for feather competition, practise on feather at least some of the time, because the timing does not transfer perfectly.

articles.title: Best Badminton Sets for Families (2026) - Garden and Backyard
articles.headline: Best Badminton Sets for Families (2026)
articles.metaDescription: The best badminton sets for families and backyards in 2026. Two-player versus four-player sets, whether you need a net, and what to upgrade first on a cheap set.

body.text: Badminton is the best garden sport there is — it needs no skill to start, no space to speak of, and a shuttlecock does not break windows. The problem is that "badminton set" describes two completely different products, and buying the wrong one is why so many garden sets end up in the shed after one summer.
Work out which of the two you need first, and the rest of the decision is straightforward.
Racket Sets and Garden Kits Are Not the Same Thing

A racket set is two or four matched rackets, some shuttles and a bag. No net. A garden kit is a net and posts plus, usually, four cheap rackets. They cost roughly the same and they are not competing with each other.

If you already have somewhere to play — a club, a park with a net, a beach — buy a racket set, because all the money goes into the rackets. If you need a net in the garden, you have a choice: buy a garden kit and accept mediocre rackets, or buy a good net and a good racket set separately for maybe forty dollars more. The second option is much better equipment and it is what we would do.
How Many Rackets

This is the decision that determines quality more than the price does. Spending $50 on four rackets means each frame cost twelve dollars; spending $50 on two means each cost twenty-five. Twelve-dollar rackets are aluminium heads on steel shafts and feel dead. Twenty-five-dollar rackets can be graphite.
So buy the four-racket set only if four people genuinely play at once. If it is usually two of you with occasional guests, buy the two-racket set and add a cheap pair later.
Aluminium or Graphite

Sets under about $45 are almost all aluminium head on a steel shaft. That construction is heavy and flexes in the middle of the shaft rather than whipping through, so shots feel mushy — but it is also very hard to break, which is genuinely the right property for equipment that lives in a garage and gets lent to visitors.
Graphite sets start around $55 and feel like a different sport. Buy aluminium if this is a social thing that happens four times a summer. Buy graphite if anyone in the house is going to start caring.
The Sets Worth Buying

Two of the Yonex GR 303 rackets in one box for not much more than the price of one. That matters because these are frames we would recommend individually — isometric heads and shafts that genuinely flex, rather than the anonymous aluminium that fills most sets at this price. Full covers included. The obvious pick if two people are starting together.

Four carbon-fibre rackets is unusual at this price — nearly every four-racket set is aluminium, and the difference in how a shot feels is immediate rather than subtle. Buy it if the point is doubles in a garden and you would rather all four people had something decent than two people had something good. The bundled shuttles are the weak link, as they always are.

A pair of genuine one-piece full-carbon frames at roughly the price of one mid-range branded racket. At 79 grams both are light enough to swing quickly through a long rally, and the one-piece construction means the head does not twist away from the shaft on off-centre hits. Buy this when two people in the house are past borrowing whatever is in the shed.
If You Need a Net Too

The nets bundled with garden kits are usually fine for casual play, but they share one failure: the poles bow inwards under the net's tension and the middle sags within twenty minutes. Standalone nets fix that with thicker poles, guy ropes, or a tensioning winch.

Height matters more than people expect. Regulation is 5ft 1in at the posts, and adults who have played before will notice immediately if a net is short. Children, on the other hand, have far better rallies with the net lowered — which is why height-adjustable nets are the right answer for a mixed-age garden.

The portable net most people should buy, and the ratings say so more emphatically than anything else in the category. It extends to a proper width, adjusts between badminton and pickleball heights, folds flat and goes up in a couple of minutes without needing a second pair of hands. Nothing about it is clever; everything about it works, which is the point.
What to Upgrade First

In order: the shuttles, the grips, then the rackets. Bundled shuttles are the cheapest hard nylon on the market and they fly flat and dead — a $10 tube of proper nylon changes the game more than any other ten dollars you could spend.

Then overgrips, at a dollar or two each, because every set racket ships with a moulded plastic handle that gets slippery the moment hands warm up. Only after both of those is the racket itself the thing holding anybody back.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Two people playing: buy the Yonex GR 303 Combo. Four people playing regularly: buy the Senston four-racket carbon set. Two people who are getting serious: buy the Senston N80 pair. Buy the net separately rather than taking the one bundled into a cheap kit, and spend ten dollars on real shuttles whatever you decide.

faq.q: Is a badminton set better value than buying rackets separately?
faq.a: For two or more players, usually yes — a matched pair costs about 20 to 30 percent less than the same rackets bought individually, with covers and a bag included. For one player it is worse value, because half the money goes into a racket that sits in a cupboard. The exception is club players who deliberately carry a spare for broken strings.

faq.q: Do badminton sets include a net?
faq.a: Some do, most two-player and four-player racket sets do not. Racket sets normally include rackets, shuttles and a bag. Full garden kits include a net and posts, but usually spend so little on the rackets that they are barely playable. Buying a good racket set plus a separate net gives much better equipment for similar money.

faq.q: What size badminton net do I need for a garden?
faq.a: Regulation is 20ft wide and 5ft 1in high at the posts, dipping to 5ft in the centre. Most portable garden nets are 10 to 15ft wide, which means the doubles tramlines do not exist — fine for casual play, wrong if anyone is practising. If space allows, buy full width; if children are playing, buy height-adjustable and drop the net.

faq.q: Are the rackets in a family badminton set good enough for adults?
faq.a: For social play, yes. They are normally full adult length, so the issue is the opposite of what people expect — children under about eight find them long and heavy. The rackets will feel underpowered and mushy to any adult who has played properly, because aluminium-and-steel construction flexes in the wrong place. That is the price of four rackets in one box.

faq.q: What should I upgrade first on a cheap badminton set?
faq.a: The shuttlecocks, then the grips, then the rackets. A $10 tube of proper nylon shuttles changes how the game plays immediately — the ones bundled with sets are the cheapest hard nylon available. A $2 overgrip fixes the slippery moulded handle. Only after both is a racket upgrade what is holding you back.

articles.title: Badminton String Tension Guide (2026): What Tension Should You Use?
articles.headline: Badminton String Tension Guide (2026)
articles.metaDescription: What badminton string tension to use and why. The power-versus-control trade explained, how often to restring, string gauge, and why copying a professional's tension makes you worse.

body.text: String tension is the most talked-about number in badminton and the most misunderstood. It is treated as a skill ranking — higher tension means better player — and that is not what it is. It is a trade between power and precision, and the correct setting depends on how consistently you hit the middle of the racket.
The short version: 20 to 24 lbs covers almost every club player, and copying the 30 lbs a professional uses will make your racket feel dead.
What Tension Actually Changes

A loosely strung bed acts like a trampoline. The strings deform further, hold the shuttle marginally longer and throw it back with added energy. That gives you more power for the same swing and a bigger effective sweet spot, because even an off-centre hit still gets some of that spring.

A tightly strung bed barely deforms. The shuttle leaves flatter and faster, and where it goes is determined almost entirely by the racket face angle rather than by string behaviour. That is precision — but it only helps if you are hitting the middle, because a tight bed gives an off-centre hit nothing at all.

So the question is not "how good am I" but "how often do I hit the sweet spot". If the answer is "most of the time", higher tension pays. If it is "I am working on it", lower tension gives you shots that still cross the net.
The Numbers

items: 18-20 lbs — beginners, or anyone who wants maximum help with power. Very forgiving, mushy feel, strings last a long time.
20-23 lbs — the club default and where most people should be. Factory stringing lands here.
23-26 lbs — consistent players who want control. Noticeably flatter response, strings break sooner.
27 lbs+ — competitive players with fast swings and a stringer on call. Almost nobody reading this needs it.

body.text: One caveat that matters: many cheaper rackets are rated to a maximum tension, often around 24 lbs, and stringing above it can deform or crack the frame. Check before you ask for 26.
Strings Die Long Before They Break

This is the part almost everyone gets wrong, and it costs more performance than choosing the wrong tension does. A string bed starts losing tension the moment it is fitted — fastest in the first 48 hours, then slowly and continuously forever.

A racket strung eight months ago at 24 lbs is not at 24 lbs. It is soft, unresponsive, and produces the vague dead feeling people usually blame on the frame. Nothing has broken, so nothing looks wrong.

The rule of thumb is to restring as many times a year as you play hours per week. Twice a week means roughly every six months. Five times a week means every couple of months. If you cannot remember when it was last done, it is due.
Gauge: Thin Bites, Thick Lasts

String is sold by diameter, typically 0.61mm to 0.70mm. Thinner string cuts into the shuttle's cork more, which gives a sharper sound and slightly better control on slices and drops — and breaks much sooner, sometimes in a single session if you catch a frame hit.

Thicker string at 0.70mm survives mis-hits and lasts months. Start there. Find out how often you break strings. Only then decide whether the extra bite of a thinner gauge is worth the running cost, because for most club players it is not.

BG65 is the string most badminton players in the world currently have on their racket, and it earns that by sitting deliberately in the middle of everything. Durable enough for club play at 0.70mm, responsive enough that you are not fighting it, and happy anywhere between 20 and 26 lbs. If you have no opinion about string, this is the correct thing to have no opinion about.

The same 0.70mm gauge with a titanium coating that makes it last longer still, which matters most for exactly the players who break strings most — people still finding the sweet spot. A 10m set is one racket's worth, so buying it yourself and handing it to a stringer avoids their markup on string. Not a performance upgrade over plain BG65; a longevity one.
Should You String It Yourself?

Only with a badminton-specific machine. Badminton frames are strung at roughly a third of tennis tension and are far more fragile — a clamp designed for a tennis racket will crush a badminton frame. Hand-stringing is not possible in any meaningful sense.

A club stringer typically charges $20 to $25 including string. If you restring twice a year, that is fine. If you or a group of you restring twenty times a year, a machine and a reel pays for itself quickly — a 200m reel is around twenty rackets' worth.

The same titanium-coated BG65, bought by the reel. Two hundred metres is around twenty rackets, and the per-racket cost drops to a fraction of buying individual sets. Completely pointless if you take your racket to a shop, and obviously correct if you own a stringing machine or share one with a club.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: String at 20 to 22 lbs if you are still learning, 22 to 24 if you hit the middle most of the time, and stop there unless you have a specific reason. Use 0.70mm BG65 or equivalent. Restring roughly as many times a year as you play hours per week, whether or not anything has broken — a dead string bed costs you more than a slightly wrong tension ever will.

faq.q: What string tension should a beginner use?
faq.a: 20 to 22 lbs, which is roughly what factory stringing gives you anyway. Lower tension deforms further and throws the shuttle back with added energy, so you get more power for the same swing and a bigger effective sweet spot. Higher tension only helps once you consistently hit the middle of the racket, because a tight string bed gives an off-centre hit nothing.

faq.q: Does higher string tension give more power?
faq.a: No — it gives less power and more control. The trampoline effect of a looser bed is what adds power. High tension flattens the response so the shuttle goes exactly where the racket face points, which is precision rather than power. The reason professionals use very high tension is that they generate their own power and want the control.

faq.q: How often should I restring my badminton racket?
faq.a: Roughly as many times per year as you play hours per week. Playing twice a week means about every six months, even if nothing has broken. String tension drops continuously from the day it is fitted, and a soft bed kills control long before a string snaps. If you cannot remember the last restring, it is overdue.

faq.q: What string gauge should I use?
faq.a: 0.70mm to start. Thinner string bites into the cork more and gives a sharper feel on drops and slices, but it breaks much sooner — sometimes in one session after a frame hit. Thicker string survives mis-hits and lasts months. Start at 0.70mm, see how often you break strings, and only then decide whether thinner is worth the cost.

faq.q: Can I string my badminton racket above the maximum tension?
faq.a: Not safely. Many rackets, especially cheaper ones, are rated to around 24 lbs, and going above it can deform the frame or crack it at the joints — and it will void any warranty. The maximum is usually printed on the shaft or the frame near the throat. Check it before asking a stringer for a number.

articles.title: Badminton vs Tennis Gear: What Transfers and What Does Not (2026)
articles.headline: Badminton vs Tennis Gear: What Transfers and What Does Not
articles.metaDescription: Coming to badminton from tennis? What equipment carries over, what does not, and why a badminton racket weighs a third of a tennis racket and is strung at a third of the tension.

body.text: Plenty of people arrive at badminton from tennis, reasonably assuming that a racket sport is a racket sport. Some of the kit does transfer. The rackets absolutely do not, and the reasons are more interesting than they look.
The Rackets Are Not Comparable

A tennis racket weighs around 300 grams strung and is strung at 50 to 60 lbs. A badminton racket weighs around 85 grams and is strung at 20 to 24 lbs. That is roughly a third of the weight at roughly a third of the tension — not a variation on the same object, a different category of tool.

The reason is the projectile. A tennis ball weighs 58 grams and arrives with momentum you have to redirect, so the racket needs mass to avoid being pushed around. A shuttlecock weighs 5 grams and stops almost immediately, so the racket needs speed, not mass — and every gram you remove is a gram your arm does not have to accelerate.

The practical consequence for a tennis player is that badminton strokes are wrist and forearm rotation, not shoulder and body rotation. A tennis swing applied to a badminton racket produces a shot with plenty of arm effort and very little shuttle speed.
What Does Transfer
Overgrips — completely interchangeable

This is the one item where the products are literally the same. Tennis overgrips, badminton overgrips and squash overgrips are identical tape sold in different packaging, and several of the best-value multi-packs are marketed for tennis. Buy whichever is cheaper.

Twelve overgrips for the price of two branded ones, sold for tennis and identical to badminton grips in every way that matters. Overgrips are a consumable — they go slick after a few weeks and get thrown out — so buying them one at a time is how people end up playing on a worn grip for months. The tack is decent rather than exceptional, which at this price is the correct compromise.
Bags — near-interchangeable

A badminton racket is slightly longer than a tennis racket and much lighter, so it fits any tennis bag comfortably. The only genuine difference is that badminton-specific bags have narrower racket sleeves, which stops light frames sliding around in a compartment sized for heavier ones. Not a reason to buy twice.
Fitness — mostly, with a caveat

Court movement, split-step timing and the general ability to change direction all carry over well. What does not is the movement pattern itself: tennis is largely lateral along a baseline, badminton is a repeated lunge to four corners with a lot of overhead work. Tennis players usually find their legs are fine and their shoulders and calves are not.
What Does Not Transfer
Shoes — and this one matters

Tennis shoes are built for outdoor hard courts or clay: a durable outsole, a herringbone tread designed for a gritty surface, and a relatively tall midsole. Badminton shoes have a flat gum-rubber sole for grip on sprung wood, a much lower profile so the ankle sits closer to the floor, and reinforcement for the deep forward lunge that badminton demands constantly.

Wearing tennis shoes indoors is also often prohibited outright, because their outsoles mark wooden floors. A dedicated indoor court shoe is the one purchase that does not carry over and should not be skipped.
Strings — not even slightly

Tennis string is far thicker and is strung at two to three times the tension. Beyond being physically wrong, a badminton frame will not survive tennis tension — the frames are built for around 24 lbs and stringing higher deforms or cracks them. Badminton frames also need a badminton stringing machine, because tennis clamps will crush them.
Technique — the big one

Tennis rewards a long, accelerating swing driven from the body. Badminton rewards a short backswing and an explosive forearm rotation at the last moment — the racket head does most of its accelerating in the final few inches. Tennis players commonly arrive with more raw athleticism than the people beating them and lose anyway, because the shuttle is gone before their swing has finished.
If You Are Coming From Tennis, Buy This

A head-light, flexible-shaft 4U racket. Head-light because your instinct will be to swing like a tennis player and a head-heavy frame will arrive late. Flexible because your swing speed with a 85-gram racket is not what it is with a 300-gram one, and a stiff shaft will not load.

Head-light and Hi-Flex, which is exactly the combination a tennis player needs while they recalibrate. The head-light balance means the racket arrives before the shuttle does even with a longer swing than badminton wants, and the flexible shaft loads without demanding the wrist snap you have not developed yet. Move to something stiffer once your backswing has shortened.

body.label: The Short Version
body.text: Bring your overgrips, your bag and your fitness. Buy a badminton racket, badminton string and indoor court shoes — none of those transfer, and the shoes are a genuine injury issue rather than a performance one. Expect the first month to be humbling: the equipment is easy to replace, the swing is not.

faq.q: Can I use a tennis racket for badminton?
faq.a: No, in any practical sense. A tennis racket weighs around three times as much and cannot be swung fast enough to move a 5-gram shuttlecock properly, and the string bed is far too tight to give any feel. You would also be exhausted in ten minutes. The two rackets look related and are engineered around completely different problems.

faq.q: Are badminton and tennis overgrips the same?
faq.a: Yes, genuinely the same product. Overgrip tape for tennis, badminton, squash and pickleball is identical and sold in different packaging, and some of the best-value multi-packs are marketed for tennis. Buy whichever is cheaper per grip — there is no badminton-specific property to look for.

faq.q: Can I wear tennis shoes for badminton?
faq.a: Usually not, and you should not want to. Tennis shoes are built for outdoor courts with tall midsoles and hard outsoles that mark wooden floors — many sports halls ban them for that reason alone. Badminton shoes are flat, low to the ground and gum-soled for grip on sprung wood, with lateral and forward-lunge reinforcement. This is the one item where the difference is an injury risk.

faq.q: Is badminton easier than tennis if I already play tennis?
faq.a: The basic rally is easier to start, and the competitive game is harder than most tennis players expect. Your court movement and hand-eye coordination transfer well. Your swing does not — badminton power comes from a short backswing and explosive forearm rotation, while tennis power comes from a long swing driven by the body. Unlearning that takes longer than the fitness does.

faq.q: Why is badminton string tension so much lower than tennis?
faq.a: Because the frames and the projectile are different. A badminton frame weighs about 85 grams and is built to withstand roughly 24 lbs; tennis frames are three times heavier and take 50 to 60 lbs. A shuttlecock also weighs a tenth of a tennis ball, so it does not need a tight bed to be redirected — it needs a bed that deforms and throws it back.
